Pliny claims to have gathered twenty thousand facts from two thousand volumes. We learn how gold is mined, the uses of hundreds of plants. Francis Bacon veut une nouvelle méthode: Francis Bacon wants a new method for knowing nature, based on observation and experiment rather than the authority of the ancients. But first, he lists our “idols”, the illusions that distort the mind: those of the human species, those of each individual, those of language, those of philosophical systems. Three centuries ahead of time, he describes confirmation bias: once an opinion is adopted, the mind draws everything back to it, keeps the cases that support it and neglects or dismisses those that contradict it.

Ce recueil rassemble les études qui ont: This collection gathers the studies that showed our judgments follow predictable shortcuts. The founding 1974 paper describes three. Representativeness: we judge a case by its resemblance to a stereotype, forgetting proportions. Availability: we estimate how frequent an event is by how easily examples come to mind. Anchoring: a number we've just seen, even one drawn at random, pulls our estimates toward it. These biases are not random errors, but slopes, the same for everyone.

Journalist Dan Gardner shows that our brain judges risks by the images in our heads, not by the numbers. A spectacular event, repeated by the media, seems frequent. Puisque nos décisions sont biaisées, peu: Since our decisions are biased, can choices be arranged to help people without constraining them? That is the idea of the “nudge”. Economist Thaler and legal scholar Sunstein show that the way options are presented matters enormously. The default option is often the one people keep: automatically enrolling employees in a retirement savings plan, while leaving them free to opt out, multiplies enrollment. Putting healthy food at eye level in the cafeteria gets more of it eaten. The authors call this libertarian paternalism.

Kahneman décrit notre pensée comme le tr: Kahneman describes our thinking as the work of two systems. System 1 is fast, automatic and intuitive: it recognizes a face, completes “bread and…”, answers 10 cents to the bat-and-ball question. System 2 is slow, attentive and costly: it calculates, checks, reflects. The problem is that System 2 is lazy and often lets the first decide. Hence our biases: anchoring, availability, loss aversion, overconfidence. The book sums up forty years of research carried out largely with Amos Tversky, who died in 1996.
